turns.question: ORP at one of our pods has slid about 120 mV over two weeks while oxygen has barely moved — still sitting near 6. Before I go tell anyone there's something organic going in upstream, how do I prove the ORP probe itself isn't the thing that's drifting?
turns.answer:
I can't check this pod's readings or thresholds from here, so I can't confirm the 120 mV slide or the DO value — but I can walk you through how the documents say to verify an ORP probe.

**Check it against ZoBell's solution.** ZoBell's is the standard solution for testing redox instruments 【7†"ZoBell's is the standard solution for testing redox instruments"】. The EPA procedure is:

1. Let the ZoBell standard equilibrate to ambient temperature 【4†"Allow the calibration standard (a Zobell solution: read the warning on the label before use) to equilibrate to ambient temperature"】.
2. Place the probe in the standard, wait for temperature to stabilize, then read 【4†"Remove the probe from its storage container and place it into the standard"】.
3. Look up the temperature-corrected millivolt value from the table on the standard bottle and compare 【4†"Look up the millivolt (mv) value at this temperature from the millivolt versus temperature correction table usually found on the standard bottle"】.

The USGS pass criterion for the equipment test is that the calculated Eh agrees with the theoretical value within ±5 mV 【11†"Check: is 'Eh within ± 5 mV?"】; the EPA post-calibration criterion for ORP is +10 mV 【2†"ORP © . +10 mv*"】. If it fails, try a new ZoBell solution before blaming the probe — expired solution is a known pitfall 【11†"Check the date on Zobell's solution—do not use solution past its expiration date."】.

**Inspect and clean the probe.** A coated platinum tip causes erroneous readings including shortened span 【19†"Coating of the platinum tip can lead to erroneous readings including shortened span (slope)"】. Soft coatings come off with stirring or a squirt bottle; organic or hard coatings should be chemically removed (light bleach or 5–10% HCl soak for a few minutes) — never abrasives 【19†"Organic chemical, or hard coatings, should be chemically removed"】. Also note that sulfide-rich water can coat the platinum electrode over hours and interfere with the measurement 【3†"Hydrogen sulfide can produce a coating on the platinum electrode that interferes with the measurement"】 — relevant if you suspect organic material upstream.

**Mind the temperature effect.** ORP readings are temperature dependent 【4†"The electrometric difference is measured in millivolts and is temperature dependent"】, and the observed potential drifts until thermal equilibrium is established, which can take longer than 30 minutes 【8†"The observed potential of the system will drift until thermal equilibrium is established"】. Make sure any comparison readings were taken at equilibrium.

One more caution: if the probe has been in iron-rich water right after contacting ZoBell's, erratic readings result from a precipitate reaction 【3†"Do not insert redox electrodes into iron-rich waters directly after the electrode(s) contact ZoBell's"】.

If the probe passes the ZoBell check within criteria, the drift is more likely in the water than the sensor — but I can't verify either from here.

An ORP probe is a passive device that detects a current generated from the oxidation or
reduction chemical substances in water. This current (which can be positive or negative)
is very weak and cannot be detected with a multimeter, or an analog to digital converter.
How often do you need
to recalibrate an ORP probe?
Because every use case is different, there is no set schedule for recalibration.
If you are using your probe in a fish tank, a hydroponic system or any environment that has
generally weak levels of chemical reactions you will only need to recalibrate your probe
once per year for the first 2 years. After that every ~6 months.
If you are using the ORP probe in batch chemical manufacturing, industrial process, or
in a solution that is known to have strong chemical reactions, then calibration should be
done monthly or in extreme cases after each batch.

Soft coatings come off with stirring or a squirt bottle; organic or hard coatings should be chemically removed (light bleach or 5–10% HCl soak for a few minutes) — never abrasives 【19†"Organic chemical, or hard coatings, should be chemically removed"】. Also note that sulfide-rich water can coat the platinum electrode over hours and interfere with the measurement 【3†"Hydrogen sulfide can produce a coating on the platinum electrode that interferes with the measurement"】 — relevant if you suspect organic material upstream.

turns.answer:
**No — 0.3 mg/L between consecutive readings does not meet the standard stability criterion.** The USGS stabilization criterion for dissolved oxygen is ±0.2 mg/L, meaning variability should be within that range across five or more consecutive measurements 【1†"Dissolved oxygen Optical/luminescent sensors ±0.2 mg/L"】. The same ±0.2 mg/L figure appears as the DO stabilization criterion in the field-parameter table 【10†"DO ± 0.2 mg/L"】 and as the surface-water reading requirement: "The reading should stabilize to within ±0.2 mg/L" 【7†"The reading should stabilize to within ±0.2 mg/L"】.

**What the documents say to do when the criterion isn't met:**

- Allow the instrument a longer equilibration time and record additional measurements 【12†"allow the instrument a longer equilibration time and record additional measurements"】.
- For surface water, report the median of the final three or more readings; for groundwater, the median of the final five or more 【12†"Record the median of the final three or more readings as the value to be reported"】.
- If variability still exceeds the criteria, either use the median of the final five or more measurements, or apply site knowledge and professional judgment to select the most representative reading and document the decision in field notes 【12†"either use the median of the final five or more measurements recorded, or apply knowledge of the site and professional judgment"】.

**On noise versus a real change:** the documents don't give a method for distinguishing sensor noise from a genuine water-quality change, so I can't answer that part from the corpus. What they do establish is that a properly performing optical sensor should hold much tighter than what you're seeing — optical sensors are described as "relatively stable" with minimal drift when kept clean 【5†"Optical sensors are relatively stable. They are able to maintain calibration over long-term deployment"】, and after calibration they generally have accuracy specifications of ±0.1 mg/L or 1 percent 【8†"Optical DO sensors generally have accuracy specifications of ±0.1 mg/L or 1 percent after calibration"】. If the variability persists past a longer equilibration period, a calibration check at saturation and zero DO would be the documented next step 【7†"Check the performance of the DO sensor at saturation and zero DO"】.

measurement methods described are used by the USGS onsite
for routine determination of DO concentrations in fresh to
saline surface water and groundwater.
The primary USGS field procedure for determination of
DO is the use of luminescence-based (optical) sensors. Opti-
cal DO sensors are considered a major technological advance
over previously used amperometric sensors because optical
DO sensors are more robust in the field environment, are not
flow dependent, and are generally easier to use while provid-
ing higher quality data, especially at low DO concentrations
(<2 milligrams per liter [mg/L]).
Optical sensor methods (section 2.0) are applicable to
nearly all aqueous environmental conditions. Optical sensor
technology is available in single-parameter DO meters or in
multiparameter sondes and can be either handheld for discrete
measurements or deployed for longer term, unattended con-
tinuous and real-time measurements.
Spectrophotometric (colorimetric) instrumental methods
(section 3.0) yield consistent results when applied to the deter-
mination of DO concentrations in oxygen-depleted waters (for
example, in certain aquifers and deep-lake horizons) and can
be used to report DO concentrations from about 2.0 mg/L to
as little as 0.025 mg/L. Noninstrumental colorimetric methods
that are available for visually determining DO concentrations
to 0 mg/L can be useful for a quick reconnaissance of DO
conditions and an accuracy check of DO-sensor performance.
Noninstrumental colorimetric methods that are available for
visually determining DO concentrations should not be used to
report DO concentrations.
The iodometric (Winkler) method is regarded as an
accurate and precise method for the calibration of DO sensors
and the determination of DO concentration in water when
performed under controlled laboratory conditions. Before
sensors that could be immersed directly in the water column
became commonly available, USGS personnel were trained
to perform Winkler titrations onsite. Standard USGS practice
no longer sanctions onsite Winkler titrations or the transport
of field samples offsite for DO determination by the Winkler
method. Step-by-step instructions for conducting a Win-
kler titration that were included in previous versions of this
NFM chapter have been removed and are not included in
this chapter.

**No — 0.3 mg/L between consecutive readings does not meet the standard stability criterion.** The USGS stabilization criterion for dissolved oxygen is ±0.2 mg/L, meaning variability should be within that range across five or more consecutive measurements 【1†"Dissolved oxygen Optical/luminescent sensors ±0.2 mg/L"】. The same ±0.2 mg/L figure appears as the DO stabilization criterion in the field-parameter table 【10†"DO ± 0.2 mg/L"】 and as the surface-water reading requirement: "The reading should stabilize to within ±0.2 mg/L" 【7†"The reading should stabilize to within ±0.2 mg/L"】.

**What the documents say to do when the criterion isn't met:**

- Allow the instrument a longer equilibration time and record additional measurements 【12†"allow the instrument a longer equilibration time and record additional measurements"】.
- For surface water, report the median of the final three or more readings; for groundwater, the median of the final five or more 【12†"Record the median of the final three or more readings as the value to be reported"】.
- If variability still exceeds the criteria, either use the median of the final five or more measurements, or apply site knowledge and professional judgment to select the most representative reading and document the decision in field notes 【12†"either use the median of the final five or more measurements recorded, or apply knowledge of the site and professional judgment"】.

**On noise versus a real change:** the documents don't give a method for distinguishing sensor noise from a genuine water-quality change, so I can't answer that part from the corpus. What they do establish is that a properly performing optical sensor should hold much tighter than what you're seeing — optical sensors are described as "relatively stable" with minimal drift when kept clean 【5†"Optical sensors are relatively stable. They are able to maintain calibration over long-term deployment"】, and after calibration they generally have accuracy specifications of ±0.1 mg/L or 1 percent 【8†"Optical DO sensors generally have accuracy specifications of ±0.1 mg/L or 1 percent after calibration"】. If the variability persists past a longer equilibration period, a calibration check at saturation and zero DO would be the documented next step 【7†"Check the performance of the DO sensor at saturation and zero DO"】.
